partners.diseaseBName: X-linked lymphoproliferative disease due to XIAP deficiency
partners.mechanism_chain: CYLD pathogenic variant —DISRUPTS→ CYLD (HGNC:2400); CYLD (HGNC:2400) —DECREASES→ NF-kappaB signaling pathway (REACT:R-HSA-569067); XIAP pathogenic variant —DISRUPTS→ XIAP (HGNC:12703); XIAP (HGNC:12703) —DECREASES→ NF-kappaB signaling pathway (REACT:R-HSA-569067); NF-kappaB signaling pathway (REACT:R-HSA-569067) —LEADS_TO→ Lymphoproliferation (HP:0002711); NF-kappaB signaling pathway (REACT:R-HSA-569067) —LEADS_TO→ Immune dysregulation (HP:0011074). Loss-of-function mutations in CYLD and XIAP both lead to dysregulation of the NF-kappaB signaling pathway. CYLD acts as a negative regulator of NF-kappaB, and its loss results in constitutive activation. XIAP also negatively regulates NF-kappaB by promoting its degradation; loss of XIAP impairs this process, leading to prolonged NF-kappaB activation. This shared dysregulation of NF-kappaB signaling results in immune dysregulation and lymphoproliferation.

### CANDIDATE DETAIL
#### 1. trichoepithelioma, multiple familial, 1  —  Tier 1 — Definitive / Highly Plausible  (fitness 0.784)
**Link type:** shared causal gene (HGNC:2584)

**Proposed mechanism:** CYLD (HGNC:2584) —DISRUPTS→ NF-kappaB signaling pathway (GO:0007245); NF-kappaB signaling pathway (GO:0007245) —DECREASES→ Apoptosis (GO:0006915); Apoptosis (GO:0006915) —LEADS_TO→ Skin tumors (HP:0002672); NF-kappaB signaling pathway (GO:0007245) —LEADS_TO→ Abnormality of hair follicle development (HP:0030101). Loss-of-function mutations in CYLD impair its deubiquitinase activity, leading to aberrant activation of the NF-kappaB signaling pathway. This dysregulation can affect both cell proliferation and apoptosis, contributing to the development of skin tumors (trichoepithelioma, multiple familial, 1) and abnormal hair follicle development (associated with MONDO:0011512, which can include hair abnormalities).

**How to falsify it:** Identification of pathogenic variants in CYLD that are exclusively gain-of-function in one disease but loss-of-function in the other, or if the two diseases map to entirely distinct pathways that do not intersect at the level of NF-kappaB signaling or apoptosis. _(variant: Exclusion of common loss-of-function variants in CYLD from gnomAD populations that are strongly associated with either disease.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of CYLD in regulating NF-kappaB signaling and apoptosis offers potential therapeutic avenues targeting these pathways for both conditions, potentially through modulation of NF-kappaB activity or enhancement of apoptotic pathways.

**Proposed mechanism:** CYLD loss-of-function variant —DISRUPTS→ CYLD (HGNC:2584); CYLD (HGNC:2584) —DECREASES→ NF-kappaB signaling pathway (WP:WP467); NF-kappaB signaling pathway (WP:WP467) —INCREASES→ Inflammation (HP:0011421); NF-kappaB signaling pathway (WP:WP467) —INCREASES→ Skin appendage disorders (HP:0001077). Loss-of-function mutations in CYLD lead to dysregulation of the NF-kappaB signaling pathway, contributing to both inflammatory phenotypes and skin appendage disorders characteristic of both diseases.

**How to falsify it:** Discovery of a pathogenic variant in CYLD that leads to a gain-of-function mechanism for one of the diseases, or a clear mechanistic divergence in downstream signaling pathways that cannot be explained by NF-kappaB dysregulation. _(variant: N/A)_

**Why it matters:** Targeting the NF-kappaB pathway could offer a shared therapeutic strategy for patients with either MONDO:0011512 or familial cylindromatosis.

#### 3. frontotemporal dementia and/or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis 8  —  Tier 1 — Definitive / Highly Plausible  (fitness 0.728)

**Why it matters:** Targeting the dysregulated NF-kappaB pathway could offer a therapeutic strategy for both conditions.

#### 5. autoinflammation with episodic fever and lymphadenopathy  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.423)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-5357786, Reactome:R-HSA-5357905, Reactome:R-HSA-5357956, Reactome:R-HSA-5689880)

**Proposed mechanism:** CYLD (HGNC:2402) —DECREASES→ NF-kB signaling pathway (WP:WP451); RIPK1 (HGNC:10121) —DECREASES→ NF-kB signaling pathway (WP:WP451); NF-kB signaling pathway (WP:WP451) —LEADS_TO→ Episodic fever (HP:0011444); NF-kB signaling pathway (WP:WP451) —LEADS_TO→ Lymphadenopathy (HP:0002717); NF-kB signaling pathway (WP:WP451) —LEADS_TO→ Autoinflammation (HP:0011072). Loss-of-function mutations in CYLD (Disease A) and RIPK1 (Disease B) both lead to dysregulated activation of the NF-kB signaling pathway, resulting in overlapping phenotypes of autoinflammation, episodic fever, and lymphadenopathy.

**How to falsify it:** If mutations in CYLD do not impair negative regulation of NF-kB signaling, or if mutations in RIPK1 do not similarly affect this pathway, then the proposed mechanistic link is falsified. Additionally, observing distinct molecular mechanisms downstream of CYLD and RIPK1 that do not converge on NF-kB would refute this hypothesis. _(variant: The presence of common variants in CYLD or RIPK1 with a MAF > 1% in gnomAD that do not cause these phenotypes would suggest incomplete penetrance or alternative causal variants.)_

**Why it matters:** Targeting the NF-kB pathway or its downstream effectors could offer a therapeutic strategy for both CYLD-associated disease and RIPK1-associated autoinflammation with episodic fever and lymphadenopathy.

#### 6. hepatocellular carcinoma  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.421)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-5357786, Reactome:R-HSA-5357905, Reactome:R-HSA-168638)

**Proposed mechanism:** CTNNB1 (HGNC:2515) —DISRUPTS→ Wnt signaling pathway (WP:WP534); Wnt signaling pathway (WP:WP534) —LEADS_TO→ Colorectal adenomatous polyposis (HP:0002672); Wnt signaling pathway (WP:WP534) —LEADS_TO→ Hepatocellular carcinoma (MONDO:0007256); APC (HGNC:540) —DISRUPTS→ Wnt signaling pathway (WP:WP534); AXIN1 (HGNC:795) —DISRUPTS→ Wnt signaling pathway (WP:WP534). Gain-of-function mutations in CTNNB1, or loss-of-function mutations in its negative regulators APC and AXIN1, lead to the stabilization and accumulation of beta-catenin, driving aberrant activation of the Wnt signaling pathway. This dysregulated signaling is a common mechanism underlying both colorectal adenomatous polyposis (Disease A) and hepatocellular carcinoma (Disease B).

**How to falsify it:** Demonstration that specific activating mutations in CTNNB1 are absent in one of the diseases, or that the two diseases are driven by entirely distinct signaling pathways with no overlap in downstream effectors. _(variant: Exclusion of common pathogenic CTNNB1 variants (e.g., present at >1% frequency in gnomAD exomes) in individuals with Disease A or Disease B.)_

**Why it matters:** Targeting the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway, a shared driver mechanism, could offer a common therapeutic strategy for both colorectal adenomatous polyposis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

#### 8. X-linked lymphoproliferative disease due to XIAP deficiency  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.399)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-5357786, Reactome:R-HSA-5357905, Reactome:R-HSA-5357956)

**Proposed mechanism:** CYLD pathogenic variant —DISRUPTS→ CYLD (HGNC:2400); CYLD (HGNC:2400) —DECREASES→ NF-kappaB signaling pathway (REACT:R-HSA-569067); XIAP pathogenic variant —DISRUPTS→ XIAP (HGNC:12703); XIAP (HGNC:12703) —DECREASES→ NF-kappaB signaling pathway (REACT:R-HSA-569067); NF-kappaB signaling pathway (REACT:R-HSA-569067) —LEADS_TO→ Lymphoproliferation (HP:0002711); NF-kappaB signaling pathway (REACT:R-HSA-569067) —LEADS_TO→ Immune dysregulation (HP:0011074). Loss-of-function mutations in CYLD and XIAP both lead to dysregulation of the NF-kappaB signaling pathway. CYLD acts as a negative regulator of NF-kappaB, and its loss results in constitutive activation. XIAP also negatively regulates NF-kappaB by promoting its degradation; loss of XIAP impairs this process, leading to prolonged NF-kappaB activation. This shared dysregulation of NF-kappaB signaling results in immune dysregulation and lymphoproliferation.

**How to falsify it:** Demonstrating that CYLD deficiency leads to NF-kappaB pathway inhibition, or that XIAP deficiency leads to NF-kappaB pathway inhibition, would falsify this hypothesis. Additionally, identification of a specific genetic variant in XIAP that causes XLP1 but does not affect NF-kappaB signaling would also weaken this hypothesis. _(variant: gnomad v3.1.2 allele frequency > 0.001 for pathogenic variants in XIAP or CYLD.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of CYLD and XIAP in regulating NF-kappaB signaling could lead to novel therapeutic strategies targeting this pathway for both diseases, potentially involving inhibitors of NF-kappaB activation or modulators of immune cell proliferation.
